title: Bayonet
description: Bladed weapon attached to the end of a firearm
wiki_lead:
A bayonet (from Old French bayonette, now spelt baïonnette) is a knife, dagger, sword, or spike-shaped melee weapon designed to be mounted on the end of the barrel of a rifle, carbine, musket or similar long firearm, allowing the gun to be utilized as a spear in close combat.
The term has been claimed to have derived from the town of Bayonne in southwestern France, although this is entirely without factual basis as the town has no history of widespread cutlery manufacture, and seems to stem from Voltaire's epic poem, La Henriade of 1723.  Voltaire was in no manner a military historian and was writing about the battle of Ivry, fought on the fourteenth of March in 1590, so the contention is tenuous at best.
From the early 17th to the 20th century, it was an infantry melee weapon used for both offensive and defensive tactics, usually when charging in mass formations (human wave attacks). In contemporary times, the armed forces of many countries armed forces consider bayonets a weapon of last resort as they are rarely used in combat, although they are used regularly for non-combat purposes such as military parades, crowd control and as utility knives.

In contemporary times, the armed forces of many countries armed forces consider bayonets a weapon of last resort as they are rarely used in combat, although they are used regularly for non-combat purposes such as military parades, crowd control and as utility knives.


History

The term bayonette itself dates back to the 16th century, but it is not clear whether bayonets at the time were knives that could be fitted to the ends of firearms, or simply a type of knife.
For example, Cotgrave's 1611 Dictionarie describes the bayonet as "a kind of small flat pocket dagger, furnished with knives; or a great knife to hang at the girdle".
Likewise, Pierre Borel wrote in 1655 that a kind of long-knife called a bayonette was made in Bayonne but does not give any further description.


Plug bayonets

The first recorded instance of a bayonet proper is found in the Chinese military treatise, Binglu published in 1606. It was in the form of the Son-and-mother gun, a breech-loading musket that was issued with a roughly 57.6 cm (22.7 in) long plug bayonet, giving it an overall length of 1.92 m (6 ft 4 in) with the bayonet attached. It was labelled as a "gun-knife" (simplified Chinese: 铳刀; traditional Chinese: 銃刀; pinyin: Chòngdāo) with it being described as a "short sword that can be inserted into the barrel and secured by twisting it slightly" that it is to be used "when the battle have depleted both gunpowder and bullets as well as fighting against bandits, when forces are closing into melee or encountering an ambush" and if one "cannot load the gun within the time it takes to cover two bu (3.2 meters) of ground they are to attach the bayonet and hold it like a spear".
Early bayonets were of the "plug" type, where the bayonet was fitted directly into the barrel of the musket. This allowed light infantry to be converted to heavy infantry and hold off cavalry charges.  The bayonet had a round handle that slid directly into the musket barrel. This naturally prevented the gun from being fired.  The first known mention of the use of bayonets in European warfare was in the memoirs of Jacques de Chastenet, Vicomte de Puységur. He described the French using crude 1-foot (0.30 m) plug bayonets during the Thirty Years' War. However, it was not until 1671 that General Jean Martinet standardized and issued plug bayonets to new fusilier regiments of the French Royal Army. In 1672, the newly raised English Regiment of Light Horse in France of the English Army was issued with plug bayonets, and when the Ordnance Regiment was raised in 1685 it was issued with plug bayonets as well.

grok_lead: A bayonet is a bladed melee weapon, typically a knife, dagger, or spike, engineered to attach to the muzzle of a rifle, musket, or similar longarm firearm, thereby converting it into a pike-like thrusting instrument for close-quarters combat. Originating in the early 17th century in Bayonne, France âwhence its nameâthe bayonet was initially a plug-style dagger inserted directly into the firearm's barrel, limiting its use to after exhausting ammunition. This design, attributed to Basque artisans or local cutlers, addressed the vulnerability of matchlock-armed infantry to cavalry charges by providing a rapid melee capability without requiring a separate polearm. By the 1670s, French forces adopted the socket bayonet, a ring-mounted blade that slipped over the muzzle without obstructing the bore, allowing soldiers to fire and then charge seamlessly. This innovation revolutionized infantry tactics across Europe, supplanting dedicated pikemen and enabling dense linear formations for massed volleys followed by bayonet assaults, which proved decisive in conflicts like the Nine Years' War and the Napoleonic Wars. Over subsequent centuries, bayonets evolved from simple spikes to versatile sword bayonets and multi-tool variants incorporating saws, wire-cutters, and field knives, reflecting adaptations to industrialized warfare while retaining psychological and ceremonial roles. Though diminished in practical combat utility by 20th-century firepower dominance, bayonets persist in modern militaries for training, utility, and as last-resort weapons, underscoring their enduring tactical legacy.
